text: Gaia BH1 is the nearest confirmed black hole, about 1,560 light years away
as_written: about one thousand five hundred and sixty light years from Earth
source: El-Badry et al. 2023, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, using ESA Gaia mission data

text: Parker Solar Probe reached about 192 km/s at its closest approach to the Sun (692,000 km/h, December 2024)
as_written: about one hundred and ninety-two kilometres per second
source: NASA and Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Parker Solar Probe perihelion announcement, December 2024

text: At about 192 km/s, travelling about 1,560 light years takes roughly 2.4 million years (derived: distance divided by 192/299,792 of light speed)
as_written: roughly two and a half million years
source: Derived from Gaia BH1 distance (El-Badry et al. 2023) and Parker Solar Probe speed (NASA/APL)

text: Cygnus X-1 black hole has a mass of about 21 solar masses
as_written: about twenty-one times the mass of the Sun
source: Miller-Jones et al. 2021, Science, 'Cygnus X-1 contains a 21-solar mass black hole'

text: Sagittarius A* has a mass of about four million solar masses
as_written: about four million times the mass of the Sun
source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2022, Astrophysical Journal Letters; GRAVITY Collaboration measurements

text: M87* has a mass of about 6.5 billion solar masses
as_written: about six and a half billion times the mass of the Sun
source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2019, Astrophysical Journal Letters 875, L1

text: The Event Horizon Telescope published the first image of a black hole, M87*, in 2019
as_written: photographed, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019
source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, April 2019

text: The event horizon of a non-spinning black hole has radius 2GM/c^2, proportional to mass
as_written: the radius of the horizon grows in direct proportion to its mass
source: Schwarzschild solution, Karl Schwarzschild 1916, general relativity

text: A black hole of one solar mass has a horizon radius of about 3 km
as_written: a radius of about three kilometres
source: Schwarzschild radius, 2GM/c^2 with the IAU nominal solar mass parameter

text: An Earth-mass black hole would have a horizon radius of about 9 mm
as_written: it would be about nine millimetres
source: Schwarzschild radius, 2GM/c^2 with Earth mass of 5.97e24 kg (about 8.87 mm)

text: Cygnus X-1 horizon radius is about 60 km (2.95 km per solar mass times about 21)
as_written: a radius of about sixty kilometres
source: Schwarzschild radius calculation using the Miller-Jones et al. 2021 mass

text: Sagittarius A* horizon radius is about 12 million km
as_written: a horizon of about twelve million kilometres
source: Schwarzschild radius calculation using Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2022 mass

text: Mercury's orbit has an average radius of about 58 million km
as_written: about fifty-eight million kilometres
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Mercury semi-major axis 57.9 million km

text: M87* horizon radius is about 19 billion km, roughly four times the Sun-Neptune distance
as_written: about nineteen billion kilometres, roughly four times the distance from the Sun to Neptune
source: Schwarzschild radius calculation using EHT 2019 mass; NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Neptune 4.5 billion km

text: Light can orbit at 1.5 times the horizon radius for a non-spinning black hole (photon sphere)
as_written: At one and a half times the horizon radius
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: The innermost stable circular orbit of a non-spinning black hole is at three times the horizon radius (six GM/c^2)
as_written: at three times the horizon radius for a hole that does not spin
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: Accretion discs in X-ray binaries like Cygnus X-1 are heated to millions of degrees and emit X-rays
as_written: heats it to millions of degrees, and it shines brightly in X-rays
source: NASA/Chandra and standard accretion disc theory (Shakura and Sunyaev 1973)

text: Cygnus X-1 draws gas from a companion star
as_written: stripping gas from a companion star
source: Miller-Jones et al. 2021, Science

text: At the horizon of a 21 solar mass black hole, the tidal acceleration across a 2 m body is about five million times Earth gravity (derived from c^6 L / (4 (GM)^2))
as_written: about five million times the gravity you feel standing on Earth
source: Derived from general relativity tidal tensor for Schwarzschild geometry, Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: For a stellar-mass black hole, tidal stretching reaches fatal levels thousands of km outside the horizon
as_written: thousands of kilometres from the horizon
source: Derived from tidal acceleration 2GM L / r^3 with Cygnus X-1 mass

text: Maximum proper time from horizon to singularity is pi GM/c^3, about a third of a millisecond for 21 solar masses
as_written: about a third of a millisecond
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation; Hamilton and Lisle 2008, American Journal of Physics

text: Sagittarius A* is about 27,000 light years away
as_written: about twenty-seven thousand light years
source: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019 and Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2022

text: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of Sagittarius A* in 2022
as_written: In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released its first image
source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 12 May 2022

text: Tidal force at the horizon scales as the inverse square of mass
as_written: Tidal force falls off with the square of the mass
source: Derived from Schwarzschild tidal tensor; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: At the Sagittarius A* horizon the tidal acceleration across 2 m is about one ten-thousandth of Earth gravity (derived)
as_written: about a ten-thousandth of the gravity you feel on Earth
source: Derived from general relativity tidal formula using EHT 2022 mass

text: Equivalence principle: in free fall you feel weightless and local physics looks like empty space
as_written: Einstein's equivalence principle says that if you are in free fall, you feel weightless
source: Einstein 1907-1915, general relativity

text: Maximum proper time inside Sagittarius A* from horizon to singularity is about a minute (pi GM/c^3, roughly 62 to 67 seconds)
as_written: the longest it can possibly be is about a minute
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Hamilton and Lisle 2008, American Journal of Physics

text: Andrew Hamilton at the University of Colorado Boulder produced simulations of falling into a black hole
as_written: made by the astrophysicist Andrew Hamilton at the University of Colorado Boulder
source: Hamilton and Lisle 2008, American Journal of Physics 76, 519; JILA visualisations

text: A distant observer sees an infalling object freeze and redshift near the horizon
as_written: you freeze and fade at the edge
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: M87* is about 55 million light years away in Messier 87
as_written: fifty-five million light years away in the galaxy Messier 87
source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2019

text: Maximum proper time inside M87* is about a day (pi GM/c^3, roughly 28 hours)
as_written: about a day
source: Schwarzschild geometry, derived from EHT 2019 mass; Hamilton and Lisle 2008

text: Inside the horizon the radial coordinate becomes timelike and the singularity is inevitable
as_written: Inside the horizon, space and time swap their roles
source: Schwarzschild geometry; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation

text: Free fall maximises proper time inside a Schwarzschild black hole, and thrusting shortens it
as_written: Free fall maximises your remaining life
source: Hamilton and Lisle 2008, American Journal of Physics; geodesics maximise proper time in general relativity

text: Roger Penrose proved in 1965 that singularities are unavoidable once a horizon forms
as_written: In 1965, the physicist Roger Penrose proved
source: Penrose 1965, Physical Review Letters 14, 57

text: Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for black hole work
as_written: in 2020 that work earned him a share of the Nobel Prize in Physics
source: Nobel Prize in Physics 2020, Nobel Foundation

text: Roy Kerr found the solution for spinning black holes in 1963
as_written: worked out by Roy Kerr in 1963
source: Kerr 1963, Physical Review Letters 11, 237

text: Poisson and Israel showed in 1990 that the inner horizon region is likely unstable (mass inflation)
as_written: in 1990, Eric Poisson and Werner Israel showed
source: Poisson and Israel 1990, Physical Review D 41, 1796

text: Hawking showed black holes emit thermal radiation in 1974
as_written: in 1974, Stephen Hawking showed
source: Hawking 1974, Nature 248, 30

text: A solar-mass black hole has a Hawking temperature of about 60 nanokelvin
as_written: about sixty billionths of a kelvin
source: Hawking temperature formula T = hbar c^3 / (8 pi G M k), about 6.2e-8 K

text: The cosmic microwave background temperature is about 2.7 K
as_written: about two point seven kelvin
source: Fixsen 2009, Astrophysical Journal; COBE FIRAS and Planck mission

text: A solar-mass black hole takes about 10^67 years to evaporate
as_written: about ten to the power of sixty-seven years
source: Hawking evaporation time formula; Page 1976, Physical Review D 13, 198

text: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
as_written: about thirteen point eight billion years old
source: Planck Collaboration 2018, Astronomy and Astrophysics 641, A6

text: Hawking conceded the information paradox bet in 2004
as_written: In 2004, he conceded that he was probably wrong
source: Hawking's presentation at the GR17 conference, Dublin, July 2004

text: In 2019 calculations showed radiation can carry out information following the Page curve
as_written: In 2019, calculations by several groups showed
source: Penington 2019, and Almheiri, Engelhardt, Marolf and Maxfield 2019, Journal of High Energy Physics

text: Susskind and others proposed black hole complementarity in the 1990s
as_written: In the 1990s, Leonard Susskind and others proposed
source: Susskind, Thorlacius and Uglum 1993, Physical Review D 48, 3743

text: The firewall argument was published in 2012 by Almheiri, Marolf, Polchinski and Sully
as_written: in 2012, four physicists, Ahmed Almheiri, Donald Marolf, Joseph Polchinski and James Sully
source: Almheiri, Marolf, Polchinski and Sully 2013, Journal of High Energy Physics, arXiv 2012
